Oil, coal, and nuclear are all cheaper than solar and wind for power generation. Or at least, they WOULD be except for regulation. The government knew they couldn't make the fuel cheaper, so they sought (successfully) to regulate it into virtual obscurity. This is especially tragic with nuclear, as it SHOULD be the most prolific power source. As a fuel source, it is by far the cheapest. When you're looking at any technology you've gotta keep in mind total costs. For instance an operational nuclear plant can generate affordable energy. However, their development is very expensive. And they also have a limited lifetime due in large part to something called neutron embrittlement. Most plants we have have lifelines in the 30-40 year range. Many don't even make it that long. For instance the Son Onofre nuclear plants that recently had to be shut down due to imminent danger lasted just 28 and 29 years. The decommissioning process is also extremely lengthy and expensive. And of course accidents do happen and that also bumps up the overall cost.

The numbers you're probably looking at are operational costs - not actual costs. Imagine a Ferrari somehow cost less to operate than a Geo Metro. It'd be like then saying that Ferrari's are cheaper than Geo Metros. That could be a reasonable statement if our Ferrari lasted long enough for the operational costs to get under the up front costs, but getting back to nuclear plants - this is not even close to the case.

Perhaps the biggest issue is that solar is a disruptive technology. It enables open competition which is a very negative scenario for established energy interests which benefit from the limited availability of oil. Before you couldn't just buy a lot of land, throw some money at it, and be producing energy. The ease of competition means that margins in solar will, in the longrun, be extremely close to cost. Compare that to oil. Exxon's gross profit margin is regularly upwards of 40%. Their most recent quarter had them with a gross profit margin of 39.63%. Every quarter last year, even with very low oil prices, saw a gross margin of about 30%. You're not going to be able to maintain gross margins of even close to 30% or 40% on solar. Unfortunately what's good for the consumer isn't necessarily good for the producer.

Nonetheless solar it is being built up, and rapidly - just not as rapidly as it could be.
